title: The Indefinite and Partitive Articles
subtitle: un, une, des. du, de la, de l', des. The partitive as the marker of unspecified quantity: du pain, de l'eau.
objectives: Recognize the indefinite articles: un (masculine), une (feminine), des (plural).
Understand the partitive articles: du, de la, de l', des.
Apply the partitive to express unspecified quantity.
Distinguish between definite, indefinite, and partitive articles.

sections.heading: The indefinite article
sections.body:
The indefinite article corresponds to 'a' or 'an' in English. French has three forms: un (masculine singular), une (feminine singular), and des (plural).

- un roi (a king)
- une reine (a queen)
- des livres (some books, books)

The plural 'des' is often translated 'some' in English, but it is the standard indefinite article for plural nouns. 'J'ai des livres' means 'I have books', not 'I have some books' in the partitive sense.

sections.heading: The partitive article
sections.body:
The partitive article expresses an unspecified quantity of something. It corresponds to 'some' or 'any' in English, but is obligatory in French where English can omit it.

The forms are:
- du (masculine singular): du pain (some bread)
- de la (feminine singular): de la viande (some meat)
- de l' (before vowels): de l'eau (some water)
- des (plural): des pommes (some apples)

The partitive is used with mass nouns (bread, water, wine) and with plural count nouns when the quantity is unspecified.

Practice from Molière's Le Bourgeois Gentilhomme:

  Donnez-moi du vin.
  (Give me some wine.)

The partitive 'du' is required. You cannot say 'Donnez-moi vin.'

sections.heading: When the partitive becomes de
sections.body:
After a negative, the partitive and indefinite articles become 'de' (or 'd'' before vowels):

- J'ai du pain. → Je n'ai pas de pain.
- J'ai une voiture. → Je n'ai pas de voiture.
- J'ai des amis. → Je n'ai pas d'amis.

This is a fixed rule.

sections.heading: Definite versus indefinite versus partitive
sections.body:
Definite (le, la, les): a specific, known thing.
  Le pain est bon. (The bread is good — a specific loaf.)

Indefinite (un, une, des): a non-specific, countable thing.
  J'ai un livre. (I have a book — one, not a specific one.)

Partitive (du, de la, des): an unspecified quantity.
  J'ai du pain. (I have some bread — not a whole loaf, just an amount.)

items.prompt: What are the three forms of the indefinite article?
What is the masculine singular partitive?
What is the feminine singular partitive?
What happens to 'du pain' in the negative?
items.answer: It becomes 'de pain': Je n'ai pas de pain.

items.prompt: What is the difference between 'le pain' and 'du pain'?
items.answer: 'le pain' is definite (the specific bread); 'du pain' is partitive (some amount of bread).
